title: Instantiating Microcrypt: Obstacles and opportunities via tailored state certification
authors: Jose Carrasco, Jens Eisert, Soumik Ghosh, Dominik Hangleiter, Nicky Kai Hong Li, Ryan Sweke
abstract: Recent work has introduced the Hamiltonian phase state (HPS) assumptions, which postulate that Hamiltonian phase states can be used to instantiate pseudorandom and one-way state generators. Additionally, it has been conjectured that these assumptions can be true, even if one-way functions do not exist. This is exciting, because if true, then the HPS assumptions provide a route to the instantiation of Microcrypt. In this work we falsify this conjecture, by proving that if the HPS assumptions are true, then one-way functions exist. While this removes the possibility of instantiating genuine Microcrypt cryptography with Hamiltonian phase states, it shows that the HPS assumptions provide novel inherently quantum assumptions for the construction of classical cryptography. Technically we achieve this via a method for the construction of one-way puzzles from one-way state generators and tailored "measure first, ask later" state certification protocols. This generalizes prior constructions of one-way puzzles from one-way state generators via classical shadows and allows us to relate properties of the one-way puzzle to properties of the state certification protocol used in the construction. Specifically, if the state certification protocol admits efficient classical post-processing then one obtains an efficiently verifiable one-way puzzle, and if the state certification protocol can be efficiently classically simulated in a certain sense, then one obtains a classical one-way puzzle, which implies one-way functions. The latter observation allows us to prove that the HPS assumptions imply one-way functions, by exploiting properties of state certification protocols for phase states. The former observation provides a new toolbox for the construction of efficiently verifiable one-way puzzles by exploiting tailored state certification protocols for pseudorandom and one-way state generators.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes the utility of Hamiltonian phase state (HPS) assumptions for quantum cryptography. The authors prove that these assumptions are too strong, as their truth implies the existence of classical one-way functions, thus blocking the realization of 'Microcrypt.' However, the work provides a novel, quantum-based toolset for constructing verifiable classical cryptographic puzzles.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the Hamiltonian phase state (HPS) assumptions can be used to instantiate 'Microcrypt'—quantum cryptography protocols that function even if classical one-way functions do not exist.
main_result: The authors prove that if the HPS assumptions hold, then one-way functions (OWFs) must exist, thereby eliminating the possibility of genuine Microcrypt instantiation via this route.
method: The core method involves constructing One-Way Puzzles (OWPs) from one-way state generators using tailored "measure first, ask later" state certification protocols, generalizing prior techniques.
model_or_system: The focus is on the theoretical assumptions surrounding Hamiltonian phase states (HPS) and their ability to generate pseudorandom and one-way state generators (PRSG and OWSG) for cryptographic applications.
key_observables: The existence of one-way functions (OWFs) and the efficiency/verifiability of constructed One-Way Puzzles (OWPs).
important_parameters: The relationship between the efficiency of classical post-processing in state certification protocols and the resulting cryptographic hardness.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption tested is the truth of the Hamiltonian phase state (HPS) assumptions.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes indicate Figure 1 summarizes definitions and constructions relating different types of state certification protocols.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the context of Microcrypt and HPS assumptions, develops a general construction method for OWPs from OWSGs using state certification, and then proves the implication that HPS assumptions imply the existence of OWFs.
why_interesting: It provides a deep theoretical link between fundamental assumptions in quantum information (HPS) and classical computational hardness (OWFs), offering a new quantum assumption for classical cryptography.
